description:
We are a team of curious problem-solvers from Kazakhstan. We’re working on a NASA Space Apps challenge using open data to build a practical, clearly explained solution. We welcome teammates who enjoy research, design, coding, or storytelling.

We also looking for members who can work with data and build models, build patterns and analyse them, along with ones who is experienced at machine learning and agent-coding
summary: Motion Lab is a public web application for exploring changes in NASA SPHEREx observations. Users search an object or sky coordinates, retrieve real images, and compare dates through blink playback, synchronized views and a difference map. Source measurements, uncertainty and quality flags help users inspect apparent changes. The MVP also includes catalog overlays, quick-look spectra, labeled reconstructions and video export. Our goal is to make time-domain infrared data easier to explore while keeping observations, measurements and scientific limitations visible.
details:
Motion Lab helps people investigate how the infrared sky changes over time using real NASA SPHEREx observations. It addresses the difficulty of finding relevant images, comparing the same sky region across dates, and deciding whether an apparent difference deserves closer investigation.

A user searches for an object name or enters right ascension and declination. A Three.js sky atlas highlights the requested direction. The observation lab retrieves images for those coordinates, with fields of view of 3, 6 or 12 arcminutes and selection of available detectors and wavelengths. Observations from the separate demo field never substitute a different selected object.

Users can alternate a selected A/B pair, inspect synchronized images, view a noise-scaled difference map, or stack comparable exposures. Matching source markers preserve context. A source inspector provides measured positions, aperture fluxes, uncertainties, quality flags and light curves. Quick-look spectra and Gaia DR3/AllWISE catalog overlays provide additional context. Catalog positions and sources detected in SPHEREx images use separate visual markers.

The scientific backend uses Python, Astropy, Photutils, NumPy and SciPy. It reads FITS data and variance, estimates background, detects sources above a 5-sigma threshold, measures native-pixel centroids and fluxes, registers images using celestial coordinates and available reference stars, and associates sources between suitable observations. It screens compatible bandpasses and marks ambiguous associations. Display images do not replace the original measurements.

A reconstruction mode interpolates measured source positions and brightness for communication. It labels intermediate frames separately from actual observations. Users can export a 10-second, 1280-by-720 WebM at 30 frames per second and share a URL restoring their investigation. The cloud version uses FastAPI, Vercel and Vercel Blob to serve the application and retain processed results.

We checked the five suggested NASA targets: Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis. Their saved investigations contain 78 real frames. Results include insufficient comparable data and unreliable target identifications, not a discovery claim for every target. A separate reference field demonstrates image comparison.

The intended impact is a more accessible entry point for students, citizen scientists and researchers inspecting time-domain infrared data. Our creative contribution combines a navigable atlas, image-based comparisons, traceable source measurements and explicitly labeled reconstructions in one browser workflow.

This is an exploratory MVP. Intermittent archive access can require a partial metadata fallback. Spectral-response, contamination and calibration checks remain necessary before interpreting an apparent change as intrinsic variability. Our next priorities are reliable retrieval and an independently validated moving-source example with suitable time separation.
